newsitem.title: UK: Bracing for austerity, Bulgaria wins EBRD support.
newsitem.headline: Bracing for austerity, Bulgaria wins EBRD support.

text.p: Crisis-struck Bulgaria, bracing itself for a period of painful IMF austerity, on Friday won renewed support from the EBRD which is backing its speeded-up privatisation plans with a special fund.
Starved for cash as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) delayed a second $115 million loan, Sofia gritted its teeth this week and vowed to accelerate the privatisation of 15 major state firms.

In response the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development has renewed its commitment to the former communist country, vowing to have its 45 million ecu ($56.54 million) "post-privatisation fund" for Bulgaria in place by early next year.

"We are making progress with the post-privatisation fund... we plan to have it set up by the end of the first quarter next year," said Olivier Descamps, director of the EBRD's country team for Bulgaria, adding the bank would select a fund manager within the next month.
Providing 30 million ecu for debt and equity assistance, the EBRD plans to raise another 15 million for the fund from investors abroad.
"We have seen more interest from foreign strategic investors than ever before," he said, adding this had increased sharply since mid-year.
"We are getting calls from very serious people looking at helping Bulgaria complete the transition," he added. "It's crisis time, therefore it's an opportunity."

The EBRD announced plans for the fund in April. It is designed to take equity stakes in newly privatised companies, and can provide loans for strategic investors with muscle -- the only ones who can take a long-term view and who have the resources to buy a sizeable stake.

The sense of crisis deepened last week amid the on-going delays. Bulgarian debt hit a 12-month low in a market that setting all-time highs. Holders of Bulgarian Bradys thought they were staring default in the face in the absence of IMF cash.
But the fears receded and prices revived after Bulgaria's central bank posted a 200 percent interest rate rise and Sofia stepped up plans to sell of banks and industrial firms.
Market players are now growing confident that the IMF will release the loan after it meets in Washington next week.

"There is a feeling that they are making progress and will be rewarded," said Neil Lockwood, emerging market economist at ANZ Grindlays in London, adding Brady prices have further to climb after news they can be used in the privatisation process.

Descamps said foreign investors were heartened by the good take up of privatisation vouchers domestically, and word that some 15 companies, in the chemical, steel, shipping, and engineering sectors, would reach the privatisation block by year-end.
But he stressed that big problems remain.
"It's a very sensitive moment -- the leadership are very much aware of the situation and they're trying to do the right thing, but there is no quick fix," he said.
"The more you postpone the corrective action, the more painful your way out will be."
